messages.subject: functions and ODEs in Stan --- design docs
parts:
Along with ode solvers, we're going to need functions to be defined
in Stan. I've created design docs for both and would love to hear
feedback from users.


Function Design: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Function-Syntax-and-Semantics-Design

ODE Design: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-Support

Both are also linked from our top-level Wiki:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki

- Bob

messages.author: 5a7d96b840c23bef
messages.subject: Re: functions and ODEs in Stan --- design docs
parts:
Hi Bob,

We (a group of pharmacometricians at Metrum Research Group) have been exploring the use of stan as an alternative to other tools (BUGS, JAGS, NONMEM, ..). We are particularly interested in the proposed addition of ODE solvers to stan and their use for pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PKPD) data analysis. Here are a few comments on the “ODE Integrator Support” page on the stan wiki (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-Support). This input is informed in part by my experience developing the bugsModelLibrary add-on for WinBUGS.

“The only robust solution to dosing is to integrate between dosings. This would, of course, require a more complicated input, with dose times and a delta for the state for each dose time.”

We concur with this approach to dealing with dosing events, but we would prefer to extend the approach to all inter-event intervals where “event” refers to dosing and observation events. Intermediate user-specified events might also be included. This permits parameters that vary with time as a piecewise constant function. This is the approach used in NONMEM’s PREDPP library and bugsModelLibrary. NONMEM and bugsModelLibrary also provide good examples for how you might structure the arguments for stan function calls. The approach is flexible and has the benefit of already being familiar to a large fraction of pharmacometricians who might wish to use stan for pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling.

“Dosing Convenience Methods: steady-state dosing (i.e. dosing at a fixed time interval) and multiple dosing specifications (i.e. one only states “I want 50 dosing events with a between-dose time of 8h and a certain amount”). Both situations frequently arise in PK modeling and can be handled analytically very efficiently.”

Non-steady-state multiple dosing of equal doses at equal time intervals is certainly a simple book-keeping matter of introducing a sequence of new dosing events. The steady-state case is another story. You could use brute force, i.e., simulate a large number of doses until apparent steady-state is achieved. A more efficient approach (usually) is to treat this as a boundary value ODE problem. In other words use a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions that result in steady-state.

Finally we encourage you to implement the ODE support in stages. Stage 1 would implement a simple ODE solver. Support for dosing and other events could be implemented in subsequent stages. This is because the stan language is sufficiently flexible that the user can write stan code that implements dosing and observation (and other) events and call the ODE solver for each inter-event interval. Thus having a simple ODE solver is sufficient for most PKPD modeling problems albeit not as convenient or efficient as having the event schedule handled by built-in code.

The attached zip file contains R and stan code that illustrates user-written code for such recursive calculations. In this case it uses the analytical solution for a linear 2 compartment model with 1st order absorption, but you can imagine that a call to a numerical ODE solver could replace the analytic calculations.

Thanks for all the stan team's efforts in developing such a flexible analysis platform.

Bill Gillespie

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: functions and ODEs in Stan --- design docs
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for the encouraging reply. Here are replies to a couple of your questions/comments:

What's an intermediate user-specified event?  We've gotten requests 
to allow arbitrary tweaks to compartment concentration --- can the 
be formulated that way?

In addition to dosing and observation events a user may want to include events such as:
  • Change in the value of one or more parameters.
  • As you mentioned, a change in the amount in one or more compartments. This is often done when modeling the amounts of substances in urine. In this case the amount in a compartment represents the cumulative amount in urine. Urine is collected cumulatively over time intervals. At the start of each interval the amount in the urine compartment is reset to 0.
In addition to events that may be specified in the data, a model may include events that cause discontinuities in the ODEs. For example one might model biliary excretion in terms of discrete events that occur at times determined by the model. Also the duration of a constant rate input (infusion) may a modeled quantity, so that only the start of the inout is specified in data. The time of the event corresponding to the discontinuity at the end of the infusion is determined by the model.

I find NONMEM really impenetrable, but Daniel and I have made 
some headway in understanding it.  I'll try looking into 
bugsModelLibrary

Yes, learning NONMEM is quite a rite of passage in our field. It's a program that carries a lot of historical baggage going back to at least the 70s. But I can't complain too much since that program and its authors had an incredible impact on the development of pharmacometrics.

I and others at Metrum would be glad to help if you have questions about NONMEM and bugsModelLibrary. This could include tutorials. 

Thanks,
Bill
